title: OTA Common-Mode and Supply Behaviour
intro: The five-transistor OTA has a single-ended output, so a common-mode input change shows up at the output even when every device is matched. Its supply rejection is also worse than a fully differential stage's.

blocks.text: Because the output is taken against ground, the CM gain is defined as the single-ended output change per input CM change, $A_{CM} = \Delta V_{out}/\Delta V_{in,CM}$. With matched devices $V_{out} = V_F$ at every CM level, so F and the output can be shorted: M1 and M2 merge, M3 and M4 merge into one diode, and the circuit is a degenerated CS stage with a diode load. Neglecting $r_{o1,2}/2$ and taking $1/(2g_{m3,4}) \ll r_{o3,4}/2$:

blocks.alt: Equivalent circuit: a diode-connected PMOS labelled M3 plus M4 from VDD to the output node, an NMOS labelled M1 plus M2 below it with gate at V in CM, and a resistor RSS from its source to ground.
blocks.caption: With matched devices the output tracks the diode node, so the OTA folds into a CS stage with a diode load and tail degeneration.

blocks.text: If the tail is a single transistor with $R_{SS} = r_o$ and $2g_m r_o \gg 1$, the CMRR is of order $(g_m r_o)^2$. Tail capacitance lowers the effective $R_{SS}$ at high frequency, so high-frequency CM noise is rejected much less well.

One might argue $A_{CM} = 0$: a CM step adds $\Delta I$ to both input devices, the mirror copies M1's $\Delta I$ to M4, and M4 supplies exactly what M2 needs. The flaw is that M3 is not an ideal mirror input: F moves by $\Delta I(1/g_{m3} \parallel r_{o3})$, so M4's current changes by $g_{m4}r_{o3}\Delta I/(1 + g_{m3}r_{o3})$, slightly less than $\Delta I$. The shortfall flows through $r_{o4}$:

blocks.caption: With matched PMOS devices this equals the change at node F.

blocks.text: Common-mode gain with a gm mismatch

With $g_{m1} \ne g_{m2}$, node P follows the input as a source follower with transconductance $g_{m1} + g_{m2}$, so each input current is its own $g_m$ times $\Delta V_{in,CM}/[1 + (g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{SS}]$. The mirror copies M1's change, the difference from M2's change flows through about $r_{o4}$, and for $r_{o3} \gg 1/g_{m3}$ and $r_{o3} \approx r_{o4}$:
Compared with the matched result, the extra term $(g_{m1} - g_{m2})r_{o3}$ is multiplied by an $r_o$, so even a small mismatch can dominate the CM gain.

Hold the inputs fixed and step $V_{DD}$. M1 behaves as a high-impedance current source, so $V_{GS3}$ stays put and node F moves with the supply; by symmetry the output follows F. The gain from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$ is therefore about 1: the OTA has poor supply rejection.

A fully differential pair with PMOS current-source loads biased from a mirror behaves differently. Both outputs again move by roughly $\Delta V_{DD}$ (if the cascode of the input devices and tail looks like a very high impedance), but they move together, so the differential output is untouched. The price is that such a stage needs common-mode feedback to set its output CM level.

items: OTA drawback 1: finite CMRR even with perfect matching, because the CM change reaches the single-ended output directly.
OTA drawback 2: about unity gain from the supply to the output.

blocks.title: CM gain and CMRR
blocks.text: An OTA has $g_{m1,2} = g_{m3,4} = 1\text{ mS}$, all $r_o = 50\text{ k}\Omega$, and a tail with $R_{SS} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. Find $A_{CM}$, $A_{DM}$ and the CMRR.
solution: $\mathrm{CMRR} = 25/0.0099 = 2525$, i.e. 68 dB (the formula $(1 + 2g_mR_{SS})g_m(r_o \parallel r_o) = 101 \cdot 25$ gives the same).

blocks.title: Effect of a 10 percent gm mismatch
blocks.text: In the OTA above, $g_{m1} = 1.05\text{ mS}$ and $g_{m2} = 0.95\text{ mS}$ (with $g_{m3} = 1\text{ mS}$, $r_{o3} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$). Estimate the CM gain.
solution: $\Delta V_{out}/\Delta V_{in,CM} \approx 0.040$, about four times larger than the matched value and of opposite sign.

blocks.title: Supply ripple
blocks.text: A 20 mV ripple rides on $V_{DD}$. Roughly how much appears at the output of (a) a five-transistor OTA and (b) a fully differential pair with mirror-biased PMOS loads, measured differentially?
solution: (a) The diode node and the output follow the supply nearly one-for-one, so about 20 mV.
(b) Each output also moves by about 20 mV, but equally, so the differential output sees almost nothing (only mismatch-induced residue).
